{{smaller block|For hem semethe that ''whoso evere'' be meke and pacyent, he is holy and profitable. ''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 170.}}

{{right|Gen. xxxi. 32.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whosoever'' will, let him take the water of life freely.

'''why'''<sup>1</sup> (hwī), ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' [Early mod. E. ''whie''; < ME. ''why'', ''whi'', ''hwi'', ''wi'' (also in the phrase ''for whi''), < AS. ''hwī'', ''hwȳ'', ''hwig'' = OS. ''hwī'' = OHG. ''hwiu'', ''wiu'', ''hiu'' = Icel. ''hvī'' = Sw. Dan. ''hvi'' = Goth. ''hwē'', why, for what (sc. reason); instr. case of AS. ''hwā'', Goth. ''hwas'', etc., who: see ''who'', and cf. ''how''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' For what cause, reason, or purpose? wherefore?
{{smaller block|Turn ye, turn ye, . . . for ''why'' will ye die?
{{right|Ezek. xxxiii. 11.}}
<poem>''Why'' so pale and wan, fond lover?
Prithee, ''why'' so pale?
Will, when looking well can’t move her,
Looking ill prevail?
Prithee, ''why'' so pale?</poem>
{{right|''Sir John Suckling'', Why so Pale?}}}}
'''Why so?''' for what reason? wherefore?
{{smaller block|And ''why so'', my lord?
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 1. 7.}}}}

'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' For which reason or cause; on account of which; for what or which; also, as compound relative, the thing or reason for or on account of which.
{{smaller block|''Whie'' I said so than, I will declare at large now.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 71.}}
<poem>''Eros.'' My sword is drawn.
''Ant.'' Then let it do at once
The thing ''why'' thou hast drawn it.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iv. 14. 89.}}
<poem>Lose not your life so basely, sir; you are arm’d;
And many, when they see your sword out and know ''why'',
Must follow your adventure.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Valentinian, iv. 4.}}}}

'''wick'''<sup>7</sup>†, ''a.'' [ME. ''wick'', ''wic'', earlier ''wicke'', ''wikke'', ''wykke'', ''wiche'', bad, wicked; orig. a noun, < AS. ''wicca'', wizard, ''wicce'', witch: see ''witch''<sup>1</sup> and ''wicked''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Bad; wicked; false: with reference to persons.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whan i knew al here cast of here ''wic'' wille,
I ne miȝt it suffer for sorwe & for reuthe.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4652.}}}}
'''2.''' Bad; wretched; vile: with reference to things.
{{smaller block|<poem>With poure mete, and feble drink,
And [with] swithe ''wikke'' clothes.</poem>
{{right|''Havelok'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2458.}}
''Wikke'' appetyt comth ay before seknesse.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Fortune, l. 55.}}}}
'''3.''' Unfavorable; inauspicious; baneful.
{{smaller block|<poem>For thilke ground that bereth the wedes ''wykke''
Bereth eke thise holsom herbes, and ful ofte,
Nexte the foule netle, rough and thikke,
The lilie waxeth, swote and smothe and softe.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 946.}}}}

'''wick'''<sup>8</sup> (wik), ''a.'' [A dial. var. of ''which'' for ''quick''. Cf. ''wicked''<sup>2</sup>.] Quick; alive. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|There be good chaps there [at the Infirmary] to a man while he ’s ''wick'', whate’er they may be about cutting him up at after. {{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Mary Barton, viii.}}}}

'''wicked'''<sup>1</sup> (wik′ed), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''wicked'', ''wikked'', ''wikkid'', ''wykked'', ''wykkyd'', evil, bad, < ''wick'', ''wicke'', ''wikke'', bad, + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>, as if pp. of a verb *''wikken'', render evil or witch-like: see ''wick''<sup>7</sup> and ''witch''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Evil in principle or practice; deviating from the divine or the moral law; addicted to vice; depraved; vicious; sin-

''biscop-wyrtil'', commonly ''biscop-wyrt'', bishop’s-wort) (= LG. D. ''wortel'' = OHG. ''wurzala'', MHG. G. ''wurzel'', root) (dim. of ''wyrt'', root), + ''berie'', berry: see ''wort''<sup>1</sup> and ''berry''<sup>1</sup>. The first element, however, has long been uncertain, the word having variant forms, ''hurtleberry'', ''hurtberry'', ''hartberry'', showing confusion or perhaps ult. identity with ''hartberry'' in its orig. application (AS. ''heortberge'', berry of the buckthorn). See ''hurtleberry'', ''hurtberry'', ''hurt''<sup>2</sup>, ''hartberry'', ''huckleberry''.] A shrub, ''Vaccinium Myrtillus'', or its fruit. {{smaller|It is a low bush with numerous angled branches, and glaucous blackish berries which are edible. It grows in Europe, in Siberia, and in America from Colorado to Alaska. The name is extended to many other vacciniums bearing similar fruit. See ''huckleberry''.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>At my feet
The ''whortle-berries'' are bedew’d with spray
Dash’d upwards by the furious waterfall.</poem>
{{right|''Coleridge'', The Picture, or The Lover’s Resolution.}}}}

'''Victorian whortleberry''', {{smaller|a prostrate or creeping shrub, ''Wittsteinia vacciniacea'', of the whortleberry family, found on mountain rocks in Victoria. It is exceptional in the order for its dehiscent anthers.}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Lose not your life so basely, sir; you are arm’d;

{{smaller block|<poem>
I am of late
Shut from the world; and ''why'' it should be thus
Is all I wish to know.
</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
I was dispatch’d for their defence and guard;
And listen ''why''; for I will tell you now.
</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 43.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
Clearer it grew than winter sky
That Nature still had reasons ''why''.
</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', The Nomades.}}}}

{{smaller|''Why'', like other words of the same class, is occasionally used as a noun.}}

{{smaller block|Cursed were he that had none other ''why'' to believe than that I so say.
{{right|''Tyndale'', Ans. to Sir T. More, etc. (Parker Soc., 1850), p. 52.}}}}

{{smaller block|Thus ’tis when a man will be ignorantly officious, do services, and not know his ''why''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, ii. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|In your Fancy carry along with you the When and the ''Why'' many of these things were spoken.
{{right|''R. Milward'', Ded. to Selden’s Table-Talk.}}}}

'''For why'''   [AS. ''for-hwī'']. See ''for''.—'''The cause why, the reason why,''' the cause or reason on account of which something is or is to be done.

{{smaller block|''The cause whi'' his Doughtres made him dronken, and for to ly by him, was this: because thei sawghe no man aboute hem but only here Fadre.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 101.}}}}

'''The why and wherefore,''' the reason.

'''why'''<sup>1</sup> (hwī or wī), ''interj.'' '''1.''' An emphatic or often expletive use of the adverb.

{{smaller block|A Jew would have wept to have seen our parting; ''why'', my grandam, having no eyes, look you, wept herself blind at my parting.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 3. 13.}}}}

<poem>
''Why'', this it is that spoils all our brave bloods.
</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, ii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|''May.'' Where is your mistress, villain? when went she abroad? ''Pren.'' Abroad, sir? ''why,'' as soon as she was up, sir.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster,'' Northward Ho, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>If her chill heart I cannot move,
''Why,'' I’ll enjoy the very love.</poem>

{{smaller block|<poem>When the church
Was taken with a ''Why-not?'' in the lurch.</poem> {{right|''S. Butler,'' On Philip Nyes Thanksgiving.}}}}
{{smaller block|This game . . . was like to have been lost with a ''whynot.'' {{right|''Sir J. Harington,'' in Nugæ Antiq. (ed. Park), [II. 144.}}}}
{{smaller block|Now, dame Selby, I have you at a ''whynot,'' or I never had. {{right|''Richardson,'' Sir Charles Grandison, IV. iv.}}}}

'''Whytt’s disease.''' Tubercular meningitis; acute hydrocephalus.

'''wi’''' (wi), ''prep.'' A dialectal (Scotch) abbreviation of ''with''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wibble†''' (wib′l), ''n.''   [A corrupt form of ''wimble.'']   A wimble. ''Tufts’s Glossary of Thieves’ Jargon'' (1798).

'''wicche†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''witch.''

'''wich''' (wich), ''n.'' See ''wick''<sup>4</sup>.

'''wiche†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''witch.''

'''wick'''<sup>1</sup> (wik), ''n.''   [Formerly and dial. also ''week;'' < ME. ''wicke, weke, weyke, weike,'' < AS. ''weoca'' (for *''wica''), a wick (also in comp. ''candel-weoca,'' candle-wick), = OD. ''wiecke,'' a wick, = MLG. ''weke, weike,'' LG. ''wike, weke,'' lint for wounds, a wick, = OHG. ''wioh,'' MHG. ''wieche, weche,'' wick, G. dial. (Bav.) ''wickel,'' bunch of flax, = Sw. ''veke,'' a wick, = Dan. ''væge,'' a wick, = Norw. ''vik,'' a skein of thread, also a bend; prob. ult. from the verb represented by AS. ''wīcan'' (pp. ''wicen''), yield, give way: see ''weak.'']   A number of threads of cotton or some spongy substance loosely twisted together or braided, which by capillary action draws up the oil in lamps or the melted tallow or wax in candles in small successive portions to be burned; also, a piece of woven fabric used for the same purpose.
{{smaller block|The ''wicke'' and the warme fuyr wol make a fayr flamme.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xx. 205.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>There lives within the very flame of love
A kind of ''wick'' or snuff that will abate it.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 7. 116.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''wick'' grew long and black, and cabbaged at the end.
{{right|''Irving'', Bracebridge Hall, p. 96.}}}}

'''wick'''<sup>2</sup> (wik), ''n.''   [Also in comp. ''-wick'', and assibilated ''-wich''; also ''wike''; < ME. ''wike'', ''wyke'', ''wic'', < AS. ''wīc'', a town, village, dwelling, street, camp, quarter, = OS. ''wīk'' = OFries. ''wīk'' = D. ''wijk'', quarter, parish, retreat, refuge, = MLG. ''wīk'', LG. ''wike'', ''wik'' = OHG. ''wīh'' (''wīhh-''), a place, locality, MHG. ''wich'' = Goth. ''weihs'', village, < L. ''vīcus'', village, street, quarter, = Gr. οἶκος, house, = Skt. ''vēça'', house, yard. The word enters, as ''-wick'' or ''-wich'', into many place-names (being confused in some with ''wick''<sup>3</sup> and ''wick''<sup>4</sup>, ''wich''). From the L. ''vicus'' are ult. E. ''vicine'', ''vicinage'', ''vicinity'', etc., ''vill'', ''villa'', ''village'', ''villain'', etc., and ''-ville'' in place-names; from the Gr. οἶκος are ult. ''economy'', ''ecumenical'', etc., the radical element in ''diocese'', ''parish'', and many scientific terms in ''eco-'', ''œco-'', ''-œcious'', etc.]   '''1.''' A town; village: a common element in place-names, as in Ber''wick'' (AS. ''Berwīc''), War''wick'' (AS. ''Werewīc''), Green''wich'' (AS. ''Grēnewīc'', ''Grēnawīc''), Sand''wich'' (AS. ''Sandwīc'').
{{smaller block|Cauntyrbery, that noble ''wyke''.
{{right|''Rel. Antiq.'', II. 93.}}}}

'''2.''' A district: occurring in composition, as in baili''wick'', constable''wick'', sheriff''wick'', shire''wick''.

'''wick<sup>3</sup>''' (wik), ''n.''   [Also in comp. assibilated ''-wich''; = MLG. ''wīk'', a bay; < Icel. ''vík'', a small creek, inlet, bay. Cf. ''viking'' and ''wicking''. Cf. also ''wick''<sup>2</sup>.]   A creek, inlet, or bay. ''Scott'', Pirate, xix.

'''wick<sup>4</sup>''' (wik), ''n.''   [Also ''wich'' (formerly ''wych''); appar. a particular use of ''wick''<sup>2</sup> or ''wick''<sup>3</sup>.]   '''1.''' A salt-spring; a brine-pit.
{{smaller block|The House in which the Salt is boiled is called the ''Wych''-house, whence may be guessed what ''Wych'' signifies, and why all those Towns where there are Salt-Springs, and Salt made, are called by the name of ''Wych'', viz. Nampt''wych'', North''wych'', Middle''wych'', Droit''wych''.
{{right|''Ray'', Eng. Words (1691), p. 207.}}}}

'''2.''' A small dairy-house. ''Halliwell'' (under ''wich''). [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|Candle-wright, or Candle-wick, street took that name (as may be supposed) eyther of chaundlers, &c.—or otherwise wike, which is the place where they use to worke them. As scalding wike, by the Stockes-market, was called of the powlters scalding and dressing their poultry there; and in divers countries dayrie-houses, or cottages wherein they make butter and cheese, are usually called ''wickes''.
{{right|''London'' (ed. 1599), p. 171. (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''wick<sup>5</sup>''' (wik), ''v. t.''   [Appar. ult. < AS. ''wīcan'', bend, yield: see ''wick''<sup>1</sup>.]   To strike (a stone) in an oblique direction: a term in curling.—{{smaller|'''To wick a bore.''' See ''bore''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''wick<sup>6</sup>''' (wik), ''n.''   [Also ''week''; < ME. ''wike'', ''wyke'', < Icel. ''vik'', corner (''munn-vik'', the corners of the mouth).]   A corner; especially, one of the corners of the mouth. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|The frothe femed at his mouth vnfayre bi the ''wykez''.
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1572.}}}}

'''wick'''<sup>7</sup>†, ''a.''   [ME. ''wick'', ''wic'', earlier ''wicke'', ''wikke'', ''wykke'', ''wiche'', bad, wicked; orig. a noun, < AS. ''wicca'', wizard, ''wicce'', witch: see ''witch''<sup>1</sup> and ''wicked''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Bad; wicked; false: with reference to persons.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whan i knew al here cast of here ''wic'' wille,
I ne miȝt it suffer for sorwe & for reuthe.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4652.}}}}
'''2.''' Bad; wretched; vile: with reference to things.
{{smaller block|<poem>With poure mete, and feble drink,
And [with] swithe ''wikke'' clothes.</poem>
{{right|''Havelok'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2458.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Wikke'' appetyt comth ay before seknesse.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Fortune, l. 55.}}}}
'''3.''' Unfavorable; inauspicious; baneful.
{{smaller block|<poem>For thilke ground that bereth the wedes ''wykke''
Bereth eke thise holsom herbes, and ful ofte,
Nexte the foule netle, rough and thikke,
The lilie waxeth, swote and smothe and softe.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 946.}}}}

'''wick'''<sup>8</sup> (wik), ''a.''   [A dial. var. of ''which'' for ''quick''. Cf. ''wicked''<sup>2</sup>.]   Quick; alive. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|There be good chaps there [at the Infirmary] to a man while he ’s ''wick'', whate’er they may be about cutting him up at after. {{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Mary Barton, viii.}}}}

'''wicked'''<sup>1</sup> (wik′ed), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ME. ''wicked'', ''wikked'', ''wikkid'', ''wykked'', ''wykkyd'', evil, bad, < ''wick'', ''wicke'', ''wikke'', bad, + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>, as if pp. of a verb *''wikken'', render evil or witch-like: see ''wick''<sup>7</sup> and ''witch''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Evil in principle or practice; deviating from the divine or the moral law; addicted to vice; depraved; vicious; sin-<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
